findings.finding: 52% of trades were accepted even though the listener got it wrong; 6 of 46 words in use now started as a mistake (misheard, or coined for something else).
findings.evidence: Wrenford "tile" = two: coined for "planks" by Ada (generation 1) · Oakhollow "tile" = two: coined for "planks" by Ada (generation 1) · Oakhollow "thathote" = five: coined for "tools" by Lark·23 (generation 23)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.43, p = 0.172, n = 12. Most used: tools (25% replaced per generation), two (7% replaced per generation), wood (4% replaced per generation); least: four (48%), five (59%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 21, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.67, p = <0.001, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
